533.title: the departure
533.hook: a king runs after a chariot, and a prince asks the driver to pretend he didn't hear
533.howItsDone: In the text, the departure from Ayodhya moves slowly, and its lasting image is the old king watching the road until even the dust of the wheels is gone.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure, part two. Bark clothes, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Did you call somewhere home for a minute? A new week begins, and today the chariot moves. Day five hundred thirty-three.

Look back, and you can't leave. Don't look back, and it feels cruel. That's the trouble with driving away from someone standing in a doorway, and it's Rama's trouble now. The charioteer Sumantra has the horses ready. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb in, with their weapons, a spade, a basket, and Sita's clothes for fourteen years. And as the chariot starts to roll, the whole city starts to run after it.
screen: `LOOK BACK, OR GO ON?` → `THE CHARIOT STARTS TO ROLL.` → `THE CITY RUNS AFTER IT.`

segments.voice: Valmiki fills the streets with noise. People run beside the wheels. Some call to Sumantra to slow down so they can see Rama's face a little longer. And from the palace comes the old king himself, on foot, with Kausalya, crying out: wait, Sumantra, wait. Rama hears his father. He can't bear it, and he can't stop. So he says to the driver, quietly: go on. If the king asks later, tell him you didn't hear. Being told to stop and being told to go, Rama says, is pain either way. Better to make it short. The chariot pulls away. Dasharatha falls in the dust. His counselors lift him and tell him something old and gentle: when you hope for someone to come back, you shouldn't follow them too far. The king stands and watches until even the dust from the wheels is gone. But the people keep following. Old brahmins, too slow to keep up, call after the chariot. Rama, out of respect, gets down and walks, and Sita and Lakshmana walk with him. By evening, they reach the bank of the Tamasa river, and the whole crowd sleeps there around them. That night Rama lies awake. These people will follow us into the forest, he thinks, and lose their homes. So, before dawn, he wakes Sumantra. They harness the horses quietly, cross the river, and the driver turns the chariot a little way back toward the city before turning again, so that the tracks will confuse anyone following. When the people wake, Rama is gone. They search for the tracks, can't follow them, and walk home weeping.

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of someone you had to leave, or who had to leave you: a move, a graduation, a hospital door, a last visit. Let the scene come back gently. Breathe in, and feel the pull to look back. Breathe out, and feel the need to go on. Neither is wrong. Let the breath hold both, the way Rama did on that road. If it helps, picture the dust settling. The bell holds the time.
The departure, part three: the road. The king runs after the chariot, the people follow to the Tamasa, and Rama slips away before dawn to spare them.
Your line: Rama slips away before dawn. Today, when a goodbye is hard, make it kind and make it short. Day five hundred thirty-three.

534.title: Guha the boatman
534.hook: at the edge of the kingdom, on the bank of the Ganga, an old friend is waiting
534.carry: a friend as dear as life
534.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Guha as a model of devoted friendship; Shringaverapura, near Prayagraj, is visited by pilgrims as the place where Rama met him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure, part three. A king running after a chariot, and Rama slipping away from the sleeping crowd at the Tamasa. Did you make a hard goodbye kind and short? Today, the Ganga, and a friend. Day five hundred thirty-four.

The chariot crosses river after river, through villages where people are already talking about the prince who's been sent away. At the southern edge of the kingdom of Kosala, Rama turns around in the chariot, faces the way they've come, and says goodbye to Ayodhya and its gods. Then they ride on to the Ganga. Near a town called Shringaverapura, the river is wide and bright. And on its bank lives someone who has heard Rama is coming.
screen: `RIVER AFTER RIVER.` → `GOODBYE TO AYODHYA.` → `SOMEONE WAITS ON THE GANGA.`

segments.voice: His name is Guha. He is the king of the Nishadas, a people who live by the forest and the river, hunting, fishing and running boats. And Valmiki introduces him with one phrase: he is Rama's friend, as dear to him as his own life. We aren't told how they met. The text simply assumes the friendship is old. Guha comes out with his counselors and his family, carrying food and drink of every kind. Rama sees him from a distance, and before Guha can bow, Rama gets down and embraces him. Then Guha makes an extraordinary offer. This land is yours, as Ayodhya is, he says. Who else gets a guest like you? Stay. Rule here. Rama thanks him warmly and says no. He has taken a vow: for fourteen years he'll live as a forest ascetic, eating only roots and fruit, and he won't break it on his first day. He accepts only one thing, and it's not for himself. Please feed the horses, he says. They belong to my father, and he loves them. That night, Rama and Sita sleep on the bare ground under a tree, on grass that Lakshmana gathers. Guha and Lakshmana sit up by the fire, keeping watch, bows in hand. It's a small scene, and it's worth slowing down for. In a story full of kings, the first person to welcome Rama into exile is a forest king, and Rama answers him with an embrace and the word friend.

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of a friend who has shown up for you when things were bad, without needing to be asked. Picture them coming toward you, as Guha came down to the river. Breathe in, and feel the relief of being met. Breathe out, and send them thanks. If no one comes to mind, picture the friend you'd like to be for someone else. The bell holds the time.
Guha, king of the Nishadas on the Ganga, and Rama's friend as dear as his own life, who offers him a kingdom on the first night of exile.
Your line: a friend as dear as life. Today, reach out to a friend who's going through something, and offer what you've got. Day five hundred thirty-four.

535.title: Guha the boatman
535.hook: two men keep watch by a fire all night, and in the morning a charioteer is sent home
535.howItsDone: Matted hair, jata, is worn by some Hindu ascetics as a sign of renunciation; in the text Rama and Lakshmana mat their hair with banyan sap on the Ganga's bank.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guha the boatman, king of the Nishadas, Rama's friend as dear as his own life. Did you reach out to a friend? Today, the night watch on the riverbank. Day five hundred thirty-five.

The fire is low. Rama and Sita are asleep on a bed of grass under a tree, a few feet away. Lakshmana sits up with his bow across his knees, wide awake. Guha comes and sits beside him. Late at night, beside someone outside the family, with the people you love asleep nearby, things get said that daylight keeps in. That's what happens on this riverbank, before the night is out.
screen: `A LOW FIRE, A BOW ACROSS THE KNEES.` → `GUHA SITS DOWN BESIDE HIM.`

segments.voice: Guha speaks first, kindly. I've made a comfortable bed for you, he tells Lakshmana. Go and sleep. My people and I will keep watch. We know this forest. Nothing will happen to Rama while we're here. Lakshmana says no. How can I sleep, he asks, when my brother, who should be lying in a palace, is lying on the ground? And then he starts to say out loud what he's been carrying all day. He talks about the old king, whom he thinks won't survive the grief. About Kausalya and Sumitra, who will be alone in the palace. About the city, emptied of joy. Guha listens, and Valmiki says Guha weeps too, as the night goes on. Two men, one grief. In the morning, Rama asks Guha for the milky sap of a banyan tree. With it, he and Lakshmana mat their hair into the coils that forest ascetics wear. It's the moment their old life visibly ends. Then Rama turns to Sumantra, the charioteer who has driven them all this way. Go back now, he says. Comfort my father. Tell him we're well. Sumantra begs to stay. Let me come with you, he says. How can I drive an empty chariot into Ayodhya? The people will think I've abandoned you. Rama answers with care. You must go back, he says, so that Kaikeyi believes I've truly left, and stops doubting my father. Sumantra turns the horses for home. Now the only ones left are Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, and a friend with a boat.
screen: `GO AND SLEEP. I'LL KEEP WATCH.` · `HOW CAN I SLEEP?` · `TWO MEN, ONE GRIEF.` · `MATTED HAIR AT DAWN.` · then, large: `SUMANTRA TURNS FOR HOME.`

segments.voice: Sit as if beside a low fire at night. Let the breath be quiet. Think of a worry you carry for someone else, a parent, a child, a friend, that you haven't said out loud. Let yourself say it silently now, in a few plain words, as Lakshmana did to Guha. Then just keep watch with it, breathing, the way two people keep watch by a fire. The bell holds the time.
Jata, the matted coils forest ascetics wear. Guha keeps watch all night beside Lakshmana and weeps with him, and at dawn Rama and Lakshmana take it on before Sumantra is sent home.
Your line: two men, one grief. Today, if someone tells you what they're carrying, just listen, and stay. Day five hundred thirty-five.

536.title: Guha the boatman
536.hook: a boat on the Ganga, Sita's prayer in midstream, and a famous boatman who isn't in Valmiki
536.howItsDone: Hindu pilgrims bathe in the Ganga, offer lamps and flowers to it, and speak to it as Ganga Ma, a mother goddess; in the text, Sita prays to the river in midstream.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guha the boatman, part two. A night watch by the fire, matted hair at dawn, and Sumantra sent home. Did you listen to someone and stay? Today, across the river. Day five hundred thirty-six.

If you've heard this part of the story in a temple or at a family reading, you may remember a boatman who won't let Rama into his boat until he's washed his feet. He's afraid, he says with a grin, that the dust of those feet will turn his wooden boat into a woman, the way it once turned a stone into Ahalya. It's a lovely, funny scene. It comes from a later retelling, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Valmiki's crossing is simpler, and it has its own quiet center.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET FIRST.` → `A STORY FROM TULSIDAS.` → `VALMIKI'S CROSSING IS SIMPLER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, it's Guha who arranges everything. He has a strong, well-made boat brought down to the bank, with oarsmen ready. Rama thanks him and says goodbye. Sita steps in first, then Lakshmana, then Rama, and the oarsmen push off into the current. In the middle of the river, Sita does something worth noticing. She folds her hands and speaks to the river itself, to Ganga, as a goddess. She asks Ganga to protect Rama through the fourteen years and bring the three of them back safely. And she makes a vow: when they return, she will worship the river with offerings. It's not a prayer we'll repeat here, but its shape matters. The first time the exiles leave dry land, Sita turns the crossing into worship. In Hindu tradition, the Ganga is still this: a goddess and a mother as well as a river, someone you can speak to. The boat reaches the far bank. Now they're truly outside the kingdom. Rama sets an order for walking. Lakshmana goes first, to clear the way. Sita walks in the middle. Rama walks last, guarding them both. Guha watches them from the far shore until they're gone among the trees. So Valmiki's boatman isn't the comic figure of the later story. He's a king, a friend, a host who keeps watch all night and provides the boat. Two retellings, two boatmen. Valmiki's is the one who stays on the bank, watching.
screen: `GUHA BRINGS A STRONG BOAT.` · `SITA SPEAKS TO THE RIVER.` · `THE GANGA, GODDESS AND MOTHER.` · `LAKSHMANA AHEAD, RAMA BEHIND.` · then, large: `GUHA WATCHES FROM THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: Sit and imagine you're in a small boat in the middle of a wide river. Feel the gentle rocking. Breathe in as the boat rises a little, breathe out as it settles. You're between two shores: what you're leaving, and what's ahead. Don't hurry toward either. Just ride the breath in the middle of the river. If you pray, you can ask for safe passage, in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Ganga, the river honored as a goddess and a mother. Guha sees the exiles across her, Sita prays to her in midstream, and Guha watches them disappear into the forest.
Your line: Guha watches from the shore. Today, when you cross from one part of your day to the next, pause for a breath in the middle. Day five hundred thirty-six.

537.title: Bharadvaja
537.hook: smoke rising over the trees means a sage is nearby, at the place where two rivers meet
537.howItsDone: Prayaga, now Prayagraj, is a place of pilgrimage; pilgrims bathe at the Sangam, where the Ganga and Yamuna meet, and the Kumbh Mela is held there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guha the boatman, part three. Sita prayed to the river in midstream, and Guha watched them go from the far shore. Did you pause between one part of your day and the next? Today, a sage at the meeting of rivers. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

Their first night alone, on the far side of the Ganga, is hard. Valmiki lets Rama's calm slip. He lies awake and worries out loud to Lakshmana: about his father, about his mother, about what Kaikeyi might do now. He even tells Lakshmana to go back and look after them. Lakshmana refuses. In the morning they walk on, and toward evening, they see something a traveler in the forest hopes to see: smoke rising above the trees.
screen: `THE FIRST NIGHT ALONE.` → `RAMA WORRIES OUT LOUD.` → `SMOKE ABOVE THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Rama knows what the smoke means. Look, he tells Lakshmana, that's the smoke of a sacred fire. A sage must live there. We must be near Prayaga, where the Ganga and the Yamuna meet. You can hear the two rivers crashing together. They follow the smoke, and come to the hermitage of Bharadvaja. Bharadvaja is a great sage, surrounded by his students, sitting by his fire. Rama introduces himself, Sita and Lakshmana, and explains that they've been sent to the forest by his father's command. And Bharadvaja, it turns out, already knows. I've been expecting you, he says. I heard you'd been sent away for no fault of your own. He welcomes them as honored guests, with water for their feet, a cow, and food of the forest, fruit and roots. And he makes them an offer. Stay here, at the meeting of the rivers. It's a holy place. It's beautiful. You can live here for the fourteen years. Rama answers thoughtfully. It's too close to home, he says. The people of the cities will hear that I'm here and keep coming to see us, Sita and me. Find us somewhere more secluded. That's worth a pause. Rama is turning down comfort and holiness, not because they're bad, but because he wants the exile to be a real exile, and he wants the people back home to let him go. Bharadvaja understands at once, and says he knows just the place. Tomorrow he'll describe it. Tonight, the three exiles sleep in a sage's hermitage, by the meeting of two rivers.
screen: `THE SMOKE OF A SACRED FIRE.` · `PRAYAGA: WHERE TWO RIVERS MEET.` · `I'VE BEEN EXPECTING YOU.` · `TOO CLOSE TO HOME.` · then, large: `A SAGE WHO UNDERSTANDS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Sit and listen. Rama knew where he was by a sound and a sign: water meeting water, smoke above the trees. Let the breath be easy, and notice what you can hear right now: the farthest sound first, then a nearer one, then the nearest, your own breathing. Rest with whatever reaches you. Each sound tells you a little about where you are. The bell holds the time.
Bharadvaja. The sage at Prayaga, where the Ganga meets the Yamuna, who welcomes the exiles, already knowing their story, and offers them a home.
Your line: I've been expecting you. Today, welcome someone the way the sage did, as if you'd been expecting them. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

538.title: Bharadvaja
538.hook: a sage gives directions the old way: a raft, a dark banyan tree, and a mountain you can see from far off
538.howItsDone: In the text, Sita honors the Yamuna as she honored the Ganga; in Hindu tradition the Yamuna is worshiped as a goddess, and Prayagraj and Chitrakoot are both pilgrim places today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharadvaja, the sage at the meeting of the rivers, who had been expecting them. Did you welcome someone as if you'd been waiting for them? Today, his directions. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Before maps on phones, directions were stories. Go past the old mill, turn at the big oak, and when you see the water tower, you're nearly there. Bharadvaja gives Rama directions like that the next morning. A river to cross, a tree to look for, a grove to walk through, and then a mountain. He's sending them to the place where they'll make their first home in exile. And he describes it with love.
screen: `DIRECTIONS WERE STORIES.` → `A RIVER, A TREE, A GROVE.` → `THEN A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: There's a mountain, Bharadvaja says, about ten kroshas from here. It's called Chitrakuta. Sages live there. Peacocks call on its slopes, monkeys and langurs play in the trees, and there are fruit and honey everywhere. It's a good place for someone who wants to live simply and well. Then the route. Follow the Yamuna until you find a crossing. Build a raft, and cross it. On the other side you'll find a great banyan tree, with dark leaves, called Shyama, the dark one. Many beings live in it, and people pray there. Walk on past it, and you'll come to a grove, and the road to the mountain. Bharadvaja blesses them, and the three set off. At the river, Rama and Lakshmana gather bamboo and dry wood, tie it together with creepers, and make a raft. Lakshmana builds a little seat on it for Sita, out of branches and leaves. In the middle of the Yamuna, as she did on the Ganga, Sita folds her hands and speaks to the river, asking for her husband's safe return and vowing offerings when they come home. On the far bank they find the dark banyan, exactly where the sage said it would be. Sita bows to it, and prays again, for Rama, for Lakshmana, for the day they'll see their mothers. Notice how this journey is being made. Every crossing is marked with a prayer. Every landmark is something holy. Bharadvaja hasn't just given them directions. He's given them a pilgrimage.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN CALLED CHITRAKUTA.` · `BUILD A RAFT, CROSS THE YAMUNA.` · `SITA PRAYS IN MIDSTREAM AGAIN.` · `THE DARK BANYAN, SHYAMA.` · then, large: `DIRECTIONS THAT BECOME A PILGRIMAGE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of the route you take most days: to work, to school, to the store. Picture three landmarks along it, a tree, a corner, a building. Walk the route slowly in your mind. At each landmark, pause for one full breath, as if it were holy. Then rest. You can walk that route differently today. The bell holds the time.
Bharadvaja, part two. The sage sends the exiles to Chitrakuta: a raft across the Yamuna, the dark banyan Shyama, and a mountain of peacocks and honey.
Your line: a mountain called Chitrakuta. Today, on a route you know by heart, stop at one landmark and give it a breath. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

539.title: Chitrakoot
539.hook: the exiles reach the mountain, build a hut of leaves, and meet the poet who is telling their story
539.carry: a parnashala, a house of leaves
539.howItsDone: Many Hindu families hold a griha pravesha, a house-entering ceremony, before moving into a new home; in the text, Rama blesses the leaf hut at Chitrakuta before the three exiles enter it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharadvaja, part two. A raft across the Yamuna, the dark banyan, and a mountain of peacocks and honey. Did you give a landmark a breath? Today they arrive, and the week closes. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

The forest is in flower. Rama walks with Sita, and for the first time since Ayodhya, he sounds almost happy. Look, he tells her, the flame-of-the-forest trees are in bloom, so red they look like they're on fire. Look at the honeycombs hanging from the branches, as big as buckets. Listen to the birds. Then the trees open up, and there it is ahead of them: a mountain with many peaks, streams running down its sides. Chitrakuta.
screen: `THE FOREST IN FLOWER.` → `TREES THAT LOOK ON FIRE.` → `THERE IT IS: CHITRAKUTA.`

segments.voice: Chitrakuta, or Chitrakoot as many people say it today, means something like the bright peak, or the many-colored peak. And it lives up to its name. Rama decides at once: we'll live here. But first, a visit. On the mountain, the text says, is the hermitage of a sage, and the three exiles go and bow to him. The sage is Valmiki. Stop and enjoy that. The poet who is telling us this whole story appears inside it, welcoming the hero he's writing about. The Ramayana does this from its first pages: Valmiki hears Rama's story from Narada, and later in the epic, Sita's sons will grow up in his hermitage. Here, he simply greets them, and they sit with him for a while. Then the work. Lakshmana goes into the forest and gathers wood and leaves, and builds a hut, a parnashala, a house of leaves, strong enough against wind and rain, with a door and a thatched roof. Before they move in, Rama performs a rite to bless the house, as a family would for a new home, offering to the gods of the dwelling. Then Rama, Sita and Lakshmana step inside. And this closes a week that carried them all the way here. A chariot leaving a weeping city. A night by the Tamasa. A friend on the Ganga, a night watch, a crossing with a prayer in midstream. A sage at the meeting of the rivers. A raft, a dark banyan, and now a home made of leaves, on a bright mountain, with a poet next door.
screen: `CHITRAKUTA: THE BRIGHT PEAK.` · `VALMIKI, INSIDE HIS OWN STORY.` · `A PARNASHALA, A HOUSE OF LEAVES.` · `A BLESSING FOR THE NEW HOME.` · then, large: `A WEEK FROM A CITY TO A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think about the place you live. Not the whole building, just one corner of it: a chair, a window, a doorway. Picture it the way Rama and Sita saw their hut the first night, small and new and theirs. Breathe in, and feel gratitude for having a roof. Breathe out, and wish the same for someone who doesn't. If you pray, you can bless your home in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Chitrakoot. The bright mountain where the exiles meet Valmiki, and Lakshmana builds a house of leaves that becomes their first home in the forest.
Your line: a parnashala, a house of leaves. Today, when you walk through your own front door, pause and notice that it's home. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

original.note: Sanskrit parṇaśālā: a hut of leaves, parṇa (leaf) plus śālā (hall, house); the exiles' home on Chitrakuta.

trapdoor: what you thought: Valmiki only narrates the Ramayana from outside.
what it means: he appears in it, greeting Rama at Chitrakuta.
what a scholar hears: the poet appears in his own work at several points, hearing the story from Narada, meeting Rama here, and sheltering Sita later, a frame that later retellers kept.
